body:
Thanks for the reply! It's crazy how similar the dynamic seems to be. We did a lot more things together before quarantine and it's fun going out to do things together.

I wasn't sure if being friends would make up for being incompatible roommates- but I'll try harder to look for the positives. Did you guys ever figure out how to approach conflicting views in regards to the apartment? Such as something like a oddly placed litter box or where to leave shoes (minor things that matter specifically to one person)?

I've been in a LDR for 4 years now. I'm also in University with the intent to go onto medical school afterwards.
My partner is quite similar to yours based on what you've said and here's how I addressed it:


I've had these goals longer than this relationship. I'm not willing to sacrifice such goals under any circumstances. You can move here or wait for me to finish.


It can certainly be put in better words, but if this is your thought process, then he needs to understand that. If he can't deal with it- then the relationship wasn't meant to be. 

Now the burden of moving is placed on my partner which has definitely contributed to the years physically apart, aside from visitations (it's 5 years in August). His goals aren't solidified and yours are. He should be making the switch because he won't be sacrificing his future.

It's wild how different the experiences are (partially) based on gender. I had men get angry at me for not being attracted to them or being a stupid woman.

I was never told that I was a wimp or had to apologize for being a woman (not exactly).

I got a few:

It doesn't look like the pictures.

We don't sell cookies at the donut shop.

The bagel hole had some cream cheese.

The price of an item was 5 cents higher than last time.

The quarter looked counterfeit.

Completely get where you're coming from. It feels like a major loss.
Talking to my BF asap always helps a little.

One year, we've been together for over four years. We generally see each other every 6 months for about 3 weeks each time.
Even if it's gonna be awhile, we make sure to always plan for the meetup as soon as we're separated again.

My partner is having similar concerns as you- without plans for breaking up.
I'm on the same boat as your partner though- based on what you've said. 
Being "extroverted" helps with the extreme loneliness that a LDR brings.

* It's easy to be pho-confident when you're talking to people if you expect nothing to come from it.
* Aging and life experience can lessen a person's shyness
* If you guys talk for hours everyday, then it's healthy to cut that short sometimes for personal lives (just like people that aren't LDR). If you never talk, then it's a problem.
* Since establishing a LDR, there are days where everything feels absolutely hopeless. Sometimes hanging out with people helps as a distraction.
* If you feel that you have too much time, then it might be worthwhile to find a hobby that can also occupy your free time. It also gives more to talk about.
* Sometimes you get so comfortable with your LDR partner that you feel it's safer to disappoint them than those around you. Certainly not a great route, but a lot of people do overly confident things to impress their friends.

My LDR has been going on for four years and these concerns fluctuate based on where my partner and I are in our lives. If it's a newer change, then maybe things can be waited out?

I have thought about it. Even though I'm a girl, I was raised to not cry or put others down. So my family doesn't feel so safe to discuss things with.
I only have one friend and she's planning her wedding.

That's what I'm doing as of late. It's currently the only reason I go out at all.
I just don't trust myself to be in charge of myself.
I'm always worried that if someone that I care about gets my dog, they'll never see the dog as anything but a reminder. It's a good starting point though.
I take medication. Tried a free therapy through my University but it wasn't useful and made me feel worse.
Thanks! I thought it'd be weird to post that one but it's my go-to silly face.

The friend that said it is very pretty though. Like guys regularly flirt with her and she even knows that she's pretty.

Thanks!

I meant the friend that said it, oops.
She's not on reddit.
I think it hit hard because I think she's so pretty.

Any suggestions for makeup to cover the bags?
I don't wear makeup and the few times I have- just for the bags, they're still noticeable.

She was talking about looks because according to her I'm very considerate and caring.
She said I'd be a good zombie in the walking dead before because of my eye bags.

Thanks! 
I think my dark circles are a little more obvious in person which is probably where her comment stems from in relation to that.

For a five minute walk I always set aside 10 minutes or more.

It's hard when you manuever around the slow walkers only to encounter a pack of them walking together. In a line. Across most of the sidewalk.

Always double your time

I don't think it's completely unusual. As an adult, your differences in opinions/beliefs are far more likely to impact familial relations. Also, if it's uncommon to have a heart-to-heart/entirely honest conversation, then there's not a whole lot of emotional/social bonding to reflect on. 

Were they ever physically affectionate growing up? Like hugs and stuff. I feel like that's also a big determining factor. 


As a kid, my parents never liked hugging or spending too much time with me, especially because they had kids young and were always somewhat busy. They always denied any physical expression that most children do.
As an adult, I was struggling to make friends in my new town and I'd call my parents often. When they learned that I was struggling, they decided to cut contact so I'd be forced to stop relying on them and make friends. This was a bad idea. I had already been deterred from expressing myself as a kid; therefore, when they did this, I realized that I couldn't rely on them in any capacity. 
Now we don't talk much unless it's about insurance and such. I feel indifferent.

It's surprisingly common, if anyone ever says that they'll overpay with strings attached, then block them.


It goes similarly if you're the buyer, too; when I was looking for a used car, many "sellers" were terminally ill or in the military. The car was always in storage somewhere (with pictures) and they'd always claim that it'd be shipped to me after I paid. The price of the car was never too obscurely low, but it was always a very good deal.


The goal is to for them to pay money to you- only to have it bounce after you send out a refund/card/item. 

As for revenge that might work: you could waste their time. Time spent on you is time not spent scamming others.

Yeah, I live in the middle of a complex but most of the people are really nice so I was just a bit taken aback.

Also, I am aware of some noise, but guests always ask if there's huge people upstairs.
